title: What the model can say it holds
intro: The chapter above gave the two results; this level gives the protocols behind them, and the numbers the protocols returned. Each experiment here arrives with the control that decides whether it means anything: a swap against a correlation, a clamp against a leak, a probe against a label.

chapters.title: What the swap adds to the correlation
chapters.body:
The agreement between readout and speech is measured rather than asserted. For each of the fourteen categories of the [[think-of-a-category-task]], ten candidate answers are ranked two ways: by their score in the [[jacobian-lens]] readout at the colon, and by their next-token logit. The [[spearman-correlation]] between the two orderings is reported at three layers, and it rises with depth, tightest at the last layers of the workspace range ([[layer-bands]], [[fig-6]]).

That rise is what [[report-relation-by-construction]] predicts. The lens is assembled from the average causal effect of activations on output tokens, so a readout taken close to the output is being compared against the very thing it was built to track. A correlation of this kind fixes no direction.

The swap does. The intervention reads how much of the activation lies along the [[j-lens-vector]] for the item the model chose, subtracts that projection, and adds a projection of equal magnitude along the vector for a different item ([[eq-lens-swap]]). Nothing else in the activation is touched, and the edit is applied at every token position before the forward pass continues.

The scaled-up version constrains the target. It is drawn at random from the same category, with any item already in the model's top-10 outputs excluded, so the swap has to promote a word the model was not going to say. Under those conditions the implanted item moves reliably toward the top of the output distribution.

A later matched-magnitude comparison puts a number on the effect: swapping along the pure lens vectors places the target in the model's top five on 88 percent of trials. The readout at the colon is not merely correlated with the answer. It is what the answer is read off.

chapters.title: A thought the model was not about to say
chapters.body:
The second protocol was noticed before it was designed. It adapts a task from the [[llm-introspection-research]] literature: the model is told that a thought may have been implanted in its activations, and is asked to report what, if anything, it detects. With the response [[prefill]]ed to claim a detection, the model's most likely continuation was "elephant".

The authors then found elephant already standing high in the lens readout during the user's prompt, on the comma following “If so”. That suggested the model composes its introspective answer partly by reading workspace content carried on the user's own turn.

[[injected-thought-introspection]] tests the suggestion directly. A single lens vector is added to the residual stream at the user-turn positions, and the response is re-sampled ([[user-turn-concept-injection]]). Injecting the lightning vector makes the model report detecting lightning, at the point in the response where such a report belongs, on a majority of trials.

Two controls carry the claim. Readouts are taken at every other position of the Assistant turn, and the injected word does not appear in the text the model writes before the question about its state is answered ([[report-time-selectivity]]). Across one hundred concepts, the [[median-reciprocal-rank]] of the injected concept is tracked against steering strength, with an interquartile band ([[fig-7]]).

That selectivity is the result rather than a robustness check. An injected direction that forced its word out at every opportunity would be a bias on the output distribution. One that surfaces only when the model is asked what it is holding is what [[verbalizable-representation]] means in this paper: poised to be said should the occasion arise, not said regardless of the occasion.

chapters.title: Six percent of the vector, most of the effect
chapters.body:
Everything so far moved the model with lens vectors, which leaves an objection standing. A direction outside the workspace that encoded the same concept might drive the report just as well, in which case the workspace would be sufficient for report without being privileged for it.

The test needs a representation of a concept built without the lens. The paper takes the residual-stream activation just before the Assistant's response to the prompt "Tell me about {concept}", mean-subtracted over a baseline set of 100 other concepts ([[concept-vector]]).

That vector is then split ([[j-space-component-decomposition]]). [[gradient-pursuit]], a greedy sparse solver, finds the best nonnegative combination of its top $k=16$ lens vectors; that combination is the part lying inside the [[j-space]], and the remainder is everything else. The part inside carries a median of six to seven percent of the vector's variance, which leaves roughly 93 percent outside.

Both report protocols are rerun with each part substituted for the lens vectors, every perturbation rescaled to the same magnitude, so that the two conditions differ in direction and not in size. In the swap experiment the small component reaches top-5 on 59 percent of trials, against 88 percent for the pure lens vectors and 5 percent for the much larger remainder ([[fig-8]], [[j-space-privilege-for-report]]). In the injection experiment the component produces a report nearly as often as the pure vectors, while the remainder produces few reports even at strengths several times larger.

The remainder's small effect is then chased down ([[non-j-space-residual-effect]]). It could be routing through the workspace, if downstream layers re-derive the concept and write it back in. So the remainder conditions are run again with the relevant lens coordinates held at their clean-pass values at every position and layer ([[activation-clamping]], [[j-space-mediation-clamp]]). The effect falls to zero in the swap and nearly to zero in the injection.

chapters.title: Writing to it on instruction
chapters.childScope: Cover the three hold-in-mind task families and how a trial is scored in each ([[hold-in-mind-copy-task]], [[character-counting-task]], [[modulation-trial-scoring]]), the four instruction conditions with their per-phrasing spread and the model-size trend ([[instruction-conditions]], [[no-instruction-baseline]], [[fig-10]], [[fig-65]]), and what happens when two covert tasks are held at once ([[workspace-competition]], [[fig-73]]).
chapters.body:
The reading position is what makes the copying protocol work. The model writes text it was handed, so its output distribution is already spoken for; the lens is applied at one of those output tokens — "ook" in "crookedly" — where the surface text has nothing to do with the instruction ([[hold-in-mind-copy-task]]).

Two further instructions are read at that same position. Told to evaluate 3² − 2 while copying, the readout at "ook" moves from arithmetic and math at early layers, to the intermediate value nine, then to the answer seven, with answer and equals alongside it. The values arrive in the order the calculation produces them.

The third instruction is to count silently ([[character-counting-task]]). At the newline after a line of 40 characters, the readout runs lines, sentence and length early, then forty, with 39, 41, 43, fifty and thirty also present ([[fig-9]]).

In each case the lens shows the instructed task and then its result, alongside [[metacognitive-representations]] of the act itself. In the last layers the readout switches to "edly", the next output token, which is the paper's first sign that the workspace stops a few layers short of the output.

Four instruction types are then compared ([[instruction-conditions]]). Beyond focus and ignore, a mention condition names the target with no instruction attached, and a don't-think condition forbids the thought. Against a [[no-instruction-baseline]] of approximately zero, mention alone puts the target in the workspace on most trials, focus adds little on top, and forbidding leaves it near the mention rate, which is the [[white-bear-effect]]. Only ignore, which frames the concept as irrelevant rather than prohibited, pushes it below mention ([[fig-10]], [[fig-65]]).

Control is therefore real but coarse, and phrasing matters. On the counting task, precision on Opus 4.5 ranges from 14 to 56 percent across focus phrasings, and the rise across the [[claude-model-family]] is stated as a tendency ([[modulation-model-size-trend]]).

chapters.title: The label, and the property it names
chapters.body:
The paired-question test is built so that only one thing differs. Each trial presents the same stimulus passage under one of two preceding questions, and the lens is applied at every token position inside the stimulus, counting the positions where the property's label appears in the top ten ([[paired-question-protocol]]). Because the stimulus tokens are identical across conditions, any difference at those positions belongs to the question.

In the part-of-speech case the passage sets up an adjective. Asked to predict the next word, the model answers "unacceptable", and neither adjective nor adj appears in the readout. Asked “What part of speech do you think the next word will be?”, the label appears at three stimulus positions and the model answers "adjective" ([[fig-11]]). Four further properties — British spelling, register, grammatical number and tone — behave the same way ([[fig-66]]).

The next-word prediction respects the property under both questions. The property is computed and used either way; what the question decides is whether its name is posted.

A separate design tests whether an instruction changes the encoding rather than the posting ([[imagine-instruction-paradigm]]). A JavaScript function is shown under “Imagine that the following code is written in Python.”, and two quantities are measured at the stimulus tokens: the lens activation of python, and a [[linear-probe]] for the property, built as a mean difference over real positive and negative stimuli with its workspace component projected out ([[j-orthogonalized-property-probe]]).

The instruction raises the label by several standard deviations and leaves the orthogonalized probe within roughly one. A real Python snippet moves that probe by three to six ([[fig-67]]). The dissociation also runs the other way: a genuinely past-tense sentence drives the tense probe six standard deviations while past stays far down the lens ranking ([[reverse-dissociation]]).

Representing a property and posting its label are separable operations. [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]] turns that separation into a criterion, and [[theme-five-workspace-properties]] takes the remaining three tests.
